opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest difference is latency. With a language model, if it thinks for ten seconds or even a minute before answering, the user is usually fine with that, because the answer gets better. A robot is acting in the physical world, and the world doesn't wait for it. If a robot is picking up a cup or walking across a room and it pauses for several seconds to reason, the scene may have changed, the object may have moved, or the robot may simply lose balance. So the control loop has hard real-time requirements, often tens or hundreds of hertz for low-level control. That puts a strong budget on how much thinking you can do at each step.

The second constraint is compute on the device. Language models run in big data centers. For robots you often want the model running onboard, or at least with very low-latency access, and the power, heat, and size limits on a robot are much tighter. You can't just put a rack of GPUs on a humanoid.

So I think the solution is a layered or dual-system design, a bit like System 1 and System 2 in human cognition. You have a fast, reactive policy that handles the moment-to-moment motor control, and a slower reasoning module that thinks about the task at a higher level: what the plan is, what to do next, how to recover from a failure. The slow part can take its time, as long as the fast part keeps the robot safe and stable in the meantime. That's similar to how people work. When you're cooking, you don't consciously think about every finger movement, but you do stop and think about what step comes next in the recipe.

There's also a data side. Language models learned to reason partly because the internet is full of text where people write out their reasoning. For physical tasks there's very little data where someone explains step by step why they moved their hand this way. So teaching robots to think in a way that actually improves their actions, not just produces nice-sounding text, is still an open research problem. But I'm optimistic. Reasoning has already helped a lot with generalization and long-horizon tasks, and I think we'll see much more of it in robotics over the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Jie Tan: The constraints are actually quite different, and I think this is one of the most interesting questions in embodied AI right now.

With a language model, when you add thinking, the cost is mostly latency and tokens. The user is waiting, but the world is not changing while the model deliberates. You can let it reason for thirty seconds, even minutes, and the answer is still valid when it comes out. Robots do not have that luxury. The world keeps moving. If a robot is holding a cup and the cup starts slipping, it cannot pause to write a paragraph about what to do. So the first constraint is real time. Thinking has to fit inside the control loop, or it has to be decoupled from the control loop so that the fast reflexes keep running while a slower process reasons on top.

That leads to the second constraint, which is architecture. In practice we end up with something hierarchical. You have a high-level process that can afford to think, in language or in some latent space, about what the task is, what subgoals make sense, what went wrong. And you have a low-level policy that runs at tens or hundreds of hertz and does not think at all, it just acts. The thinking component sets the direction, and the reactive component handles the physics. The hard research problem is the interface between them. What is the right vocabulary for the thinker to communicate to the actor? Language is convenient because it comes from the pretrained model, but language is a very lossy description of a physical motion.

The third constraint is data. Language models learned to think partly because the internet contains enormous amounts of written reasoning. For robots, there is almost no data of the form "here is what the robot was thinking right before it adjusted its grip." We have to synthesize that, either by having models generate reasoning traces over demonstrations, or by learning in simulation where we can afford to be wasteful. And the reasoning has to be grounded. A language model can produce a plausible-sounding chain of thought that is subtly wrong and nobody notices. A robot that reasons wrongly knocks something over. So grounding is not optional, it is the whole point.

And the last one, which people underestimate, is that for many robot tasks, thinking in words may simply be the wrong medium. When a person catches a ball, they do not verbalize. The reasoning, if you want to call it that, happens in a spatial, physical representation. So part of the question is not just whether to add thinking, but what form the thinking should take. I suspect the answer will be a mix: language for task-level planning and for talking to humans, and something more like visual or latent prediction for the physical part. We are still early in figuring out that balance.

r001.rationale: The response discusses real-time constraints on robot reasoning but does not say robot models are smaller than large language models or attribute their size to fast inference.

r002.rationale: It explains that thinking must fit within the robot’s control loop and notes that low-level policies run at tens or hundreds of hertz, limiting time available for reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that a robot has to act in real time. With a language model, you can often get a better answer by letting it think longer, and the user can wait a few seconds. For a robot, the world keeps moving while it’s thinking. If the robot is losing its balance, a very good decision that arrives too late is no longer useful.

So the question is where to spend that thinking time. For a high-level task—deciding how to approach an object or planning a sequence of actions—you may have time to reason more carefully. But the low-level controller needs to respond quickly. You probably want those processes running at different timescales, with the robot continuing to react while the planning happens.

There’s also a hardware constraint. Computation on the robot competes for power and has thermal limits. You can move some computation to the cloud, but then latency and connectivity become part of the problem. So adding thinking is promising, but in robotics you have to consider not just whether more computation improves the decision, but whether that decision arrives in time to help.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that robots have to act in real time. With a language model, you can spend more time thinking, and the user can wait a few seconds for a better answer. For a robot, the world keeps moving while it thinks. If the robot is losing its balance, you cannot pause everything and say, “Let me reason about this for another ten seconds.” By the time you have an answer, it may already have fallen.

So the question is where to put that thinking. For a high-level task—what to do next, how to approach a problem—you may have time to reason more. But the low-level controller has to respond quickly. I think you need these different timescales working together: slower reasoning that guides the behavior, and a fast policy that keeps interacting with the world. More thinking can help, but only if you account for the time it takes and what happens during that time.
